extracted.intended_audience: government economists and regulatory analysts preparing regulatory impact analyses (RIAs) and discount rate estimates for rulemakings
extracted.subtask_short: estimating social rate of time preference
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting and calculating the Social Rate of Time Preference (SRTP) used to discount benefits and costs in U.S. federal regulatory analyses, including data sources, averaging windows, risk and liquidity adjustments, inflation index choice, and update procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of long-duration government bond yields (Treasuries/TIPS) rather than corporate bond yields
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate bond yields add little relevant insight beyond long-duration government bond yields because variation in corporate yields largely reflects default risk and time-varying risk premia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on corporate bond yields to estimate the SRTP; long-duration government bond yields (e.g., TIPS) are preferred because non-Treasury yields are driven primarily by default risk and changing risk premia that are not appropriate for the risk-free SRTP. See discussion under 'Accounting for Risk When Discounting.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use TIPS when available instead of Treasuries minus CPI
rubrics_metrics.description: TIPS offer protection against inflation risk by indexing principal to CPI inflation; using TIPS when available yields a more consistent ex-ante measure of real rates than combining nominal Treasuries with ex-post CPI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When TIPS data exist (post-2003), use TIPS yields for SRTP estimation rather than 10-year Treasuries less CPI. The Preamble retained the approach of using TIPS where available; commenters largely supported this. Consider other ex-ante measures only as complementary (e.g., inflation expectation surveys) but TIPS are primary when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for business cycle effects cautiously (use long retrospective averages rather than short-term market conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-term events (recessions, monetary policy episodes) do not justify substantial deviation from a long retrospective average; the SRTP should capture longer-run real rates rather than transient market conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not upweight SRTP because of recessionary periods in the averaging window. Use model-based estimates (e.g., Laubach-Williams, Del Negro et al.) as checks, but the 30-year retrospective average of (10-year) real yields is preferred for simplicity and transparency unless strong evidence justifies otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not exclude anomalously low TIPS years (flight-to-safety) from the averaging window
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing unusually low years (or only removing low years) from a retrospective average biases the SRTP upward and defeats the purpose of smoothing year-to-year volatility via averaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain all years in the retrospective averaging window (e.g., 30 years). Selective omission of low (or high) years undermines the rationale for a retrospective average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquidity premia should not be separately added when benefits/costs are measured in WTP/WTA
rubrics_metrics.description: Because regulatory benefits and costs are valued via willingness-to-pay (WTP) and willingness-to-accept (WTA), which already reflect the liquidity characteristics of the underlying good or service, applying an additional liquidity premium to the SRTP would generally double-count illiquidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer an instrument with zero liquidity premium as the SRTP benchmark; recognize TIPS have a positive liquidity premium (around 30bp average) but do not currently adjust SRTP for this because liquidity premia vary over the business cycle and across measurement approaches. Do not add a liquidity premium to discount health and other non-tradable regulatory benefits valued by WTP/WTA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of inflation index: use PCE rather than CPI for SRTP adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: PCE better accounts for consumer substitution and is closer to an ideal index of money’s purchasing power for pricing nominal bonds; using CPI biases SRTP estimates downward relative to PCE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a constant CPI–PCE differential adjustment of 0.3% when converting CPI-based measures to PCE-equivalent values. Averaging CPI and PCE is a simple option but OMB prefers model- or series-based adjustments (Janson et al. approach) that justify the 0.3% adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of instrument duration: use 10-year TIPS rather than longer-duration instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer-dated assets (e.g., 30-year bonds) may reflect term premia (compensation for long-term bond value fluctuation) rather than distinctive longer-run social time preferences; data availability for longer instruments is also more limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continue using 10-year TIPS for the SRTP. Do not substitute 30-year yields without accounting for term premia; if a regulation has an especially long horizon, consider additional analysis but recognize higher yields on 30-year instruments likely reflect term premia, not a higher SRTP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default risk: Treasuries/TIPS are not perfectly risk-free but substituting other instruments or adjusting for default risk is not generally warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: TIPS reduce inflation risk but are not entirely free of default risk; however, attempting to adjust SRTP for market valuations of default risk (or substituting alternative instruments) would produce administrability costs and potential errors that outweigh benefits unless U.S. default risk rises materially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize slight upward bias from default risk in TIPS, but do not attempt routine adjustments for default risk. Reevaluate only if market perceptions of U.S. default risk appreciably increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-tax versus post-tax yields: use pre-tax returns but recognize small upward bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Using before-tax yields upwardly biases the SRTP relative to after-tax yields, but estimating the appropriate tax adjustment is resource-intensive and its magnitude is small for much of the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre-tax return for SRTP estimation (as in the proposed revisions) because marginal tax rate on interest is modest for much of the population and borrowers cannot deduct personal interest; do not routinely adjust to after-tax yields given administrability concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of retrospective averaging window: retain a 30-year retrospective average
rubrics_metrics.description: A 30-year retrospective average balances capturing changes in the long-run natural rate (r*) with limiting year-to-year volatility; its simplicity and transparency make it appropriate for Circular A-4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a 30-year averaging window for SRTP estimation. Longer windows reduce responsiveness to changes in r*; shorter windows introduce greater business-cycle volatility. Use model-based estimates only as complementary checks because they depend on modeling assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating frequency and rounding of SRTP estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Update frequency and the degree of rounding affect perceived precision and stability of the SRTP; rounding to tenths and updating regularly reduces disruptive changes while improving accuracy over older, coarser rounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round the SRTP to the tenths place and update approximately every three years (OMB finds three-year updates consistent with the 30-year averaging approach). This reduces instability from small underlying changes and avoids large jumps due solely to coarse rounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for risk when discounting: separate expected default component from risk premia
rubrics_metrics.description: Default risk is a component of loan pricing (expected value), while risk preferences produce a risk premium (spread between risk-free and risk-inclusive rates); risk-inclusive market rates therefore are not an appropriate guide to the risk-free SRTP without separation of these components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating SRTP, avoid using risk-inclusive rates that confound default risk and risk premia. Use instruments and methods that isolate the risk-free (or closest proxy) real rate; consult 'Accounting for Risk When Discounting' guidance for technical treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of observed higher discounting among low-income individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters suggested increasing discounting for low-income individuals based on observed high-interest borrowing or behavioral patterns; OMB notes other factors (behavioral biases, information asymmetries, value of other services) may explain such behavior, and that risk-inclusive rates (e.g., high interest on payday loans) reflect default risk and are not an appropriate guide to SRTP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not increase SRTP based on observed high-interest borrowing rates of low-income individuals; instead, consider alternative explanations (behavioral/information) and treat standard SRTP consistently. See related discussion on WTP/WTA valuation and double-counting risks.
